newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Yugo says ability to pay key to any Lon club deal.
newsitem.headline: Yugo says ability to pay key to any Lon club deal.

text.p: Yugoslavia is willing to clinch a debt-rescheduling deal with its London club creditors but will only accept a model taking into account its real ability to pay, a senior government official said on Saturday.

"Ability to pay is the key. We cannot go beyond that and agree to something based on assumptions and then default. We do not want to default because we would never be excused for that. So, there will be no promises which we cannot deliver," Yugoslav Deputy Prime Minister Danko Djunic told Reuters.
Djunic spoke after hosting two-day talks between the Yugoslav government and co-chairs and economists of the International Coordination Committee of commercial banks.
The two sides on Friday issued a joint statement saying some progress has been made and that they would meet again at the end of August.
The London club delegation included representatives from Chase Manhattan, Societe Generale and Westdeutsche Landesbank who came for additional economic details to be tested by their economists.

"Their visit was part of our previous agreement. Talks were absolutely open and they were given the latest economic forecasts and indicators. We also discussed our basic offer and our concept based on Yugoslavia's ability to pay," Djunic said.

Belgrade asked in mid-June for an 80 percent write-off of its outstanding $2.4 billion debt to commercial banks and restructuring of the remaining $481 million via a 25-year syndicated loan with a 9-year grace period.
"Our offer is a result of reality and a consequence of past five years. We cannot embellish the reality," he said.

Yugoslavia, starved of capital after almost four years of war-related sanctions, remains financially isolated by the outer wall of sanctions banning it from access either to official funds through the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and the World Bank or the international capital markets.

The country's economy, blighted with huge trade, fiscal, employment, inter-company deficits and a $10 billion external debt, operates below 50 percent of its pre-1991 levels with almost 50 percent of its labour out of work.
Djunic insisted up to $500 million was the best the country could offer to its commercial lenders.

"This is the essence of our proposal, the realistic capacity to service the debt. Our economic strength and capacities are our key limits. Once we agree on our ability to pay we shall discuss various repayment models," Djunic said.

A recent report prepared by the London-based Banque National de Paris (BNP) said Yugoslavia's mounting economic deficits had forced it into a corner where ability to pay dictated the terms of any future deal.
A longer term view based on the country's economic performance indicated that without a write-off Yugoslavia would lurch from crisis to crisis.
Yugoslavia -- now comprising only Serbia and Montenegro -- is the only part of the former Balkan federation not to have rescheduled its section of the 1988 New Financing Agreement (NFA) debt.

According to an international banking source, NFA debt currently sells at 37-38 cents per dollar but the price would fall as low as 23 cents if creditors agreed to a debt-forgiveness beyond 40 percent.

A deal with the London club would help Belgrade repair its ties with the IMF and the World bank, allow the country access to international capital markets and pave the way for a net foreign inflow of capital, BNP said in its Yugoslavian Strategic Outlook.

Djunic said earlier Yugoslavia would start paying back only after rejoining the IMF, which seemed unlikely to happen by the end of 1997. Relations with the IMF are at a low point because of concerns in the West over what is seen as Belgrade's reluctance to fully implement the Dayton peace agreement.
